options.denominator: None; annual count of pedestrians reported injured (pedestrians killed reported separately)
options.reason: Injury counts show the annual nonfatal harm burden directly and are easy to compare across years.
options.answer: The file cannot establish whether risk per walking trip improved; it shows reported pedestrian injuries fell 22.1%, from 3,641 in 2013 to 2,835 in 2025, after rising from the 2020 low.
options.interpretation: This framing answers whether the annual number of pedestrians injured has declined: it was lower in 2025 than in 2013, after rising from a 2020 low. Counts are a direct measure of nonfatal harm and provide a clear year-to-year trend. It does not measure risk per walking trip or explain changes in pedestrian exposure.

options.denominator: None; annual count of pedestrians reported killed
options.reason: Fatalities isolate the most severe pedestrian outcome, which can move differently from injuries.
options.answer: The file cannot establish whether risk per walking trip improved; reported pedestrian deaths rose 30.0%, from 30 in 2013 to 39 in 2025.
options.interpretation: This framing answers the question for the most severe outcome: the 2025 death count exceeded 2013, despite substantial year-to-year variation. Fatalities are a distinct and consequential safety outcome, so it is defensible to examine them separately. The count does not show pedestrian risk per trip or whether the trend reflects changes in walking volume.

options.metric: Share of reported Brooklyn crashes with a pedestrian injured or killed
options.denominator: All police-reported motor vehicle crashes with Brooklyn recorded as borough
options.reason: The share places pedestrian-harm crashes in the context of all reported crashes, rather than showing counts alone.
options.answer: The file cannot establish whether risk per walking trip improved; pedestrian-harm crashes rose from 7.4% of reported Brooklyn crashes in 2013 to 11.4% in 2025 (+3.9 percentage points).
options.interpretation: This framing answers whether pedestrian-injury-or-death crashes became a larger part of Brooklyn's reported crash record: their share rose from 2013 to 2025. It is a defensible relative measure when the overall number of recorded crashes changes substantially. It is not a pedestrian exposure rate and misses pedestrian-involved crashes with no reported pedestrian injury or death.

answer:
The data cannot establish whether pedestrian risk per walking trip improved, but reported Brooklyn pedestrian injuries fell 22.1%, from 3,641 in 2013 to 2,835 in 2025, after rising from a 2020 low (`out/option_1.png`).
The data cannot establish whether pedestrian risk per walking trip improved, but reported pedestrian deaths rose 30%, from 30 in 2013 to 39 in 2025 (`out/option_2.png`).
